screens.title: Core Components of Hyperledger Fabric Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we map the essential components that make Hyperledger Fabric a modular, permissioned blockchain platform. You will learn what peers do, how endorsing and committing roles differ, why anchor peers matter for cross-organization communication, and how the ordering service establishes a single, immutable sequence of transactions without executing business logic. We'll also explain identity management via Certificate Authorities and Membership Service Providers, the purpose of channels for private data partitioning, and how chaincode and the ledger interact to represent business logic and state. A concrete example you'll use throughout is a two-organization channel where both organizations must endorse a trade: we will trace a transaction from proposal to endorsement, through ordering and finally to ledger commit and world state update. Common misunderstandings we’ll clear up include confusing ordering with execution, and assuming channels are mere access controls rather than separate ledgers. By the end you should be able to describe each component’s responsibility and reason about a basic Fabric topology for a consortium. Consider how these pieces separate concerns: identity, execution, ordering, and storage — why is that helpful for governance and scaling?

keyIdea.title: Why architecture matters
keyIdea.text: Fabric separates identity, endorsement, ordering, and storage so organizations can control privacy, governance, and performance independently.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Core Components
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Core Components of Fabric

Understand how peers, orderers, CAs, MSPs, channels, chaincode, and the ledger coordinate to process transactions securely in a permissioned network.

Peer Roles
Endorse, commit, and discover
Ordering Service
Sequence without execution
Identity
CAs and MSPs govern who can do what
Ledger
Blockchain history + world state
Example: A client from Org1 requests endorsement from Org1 and Org2. Those peers simulate and sign, the orderer sequences the signed proposal, and committing peers update their ledgers and world state once validated.
Visual Concept
Network snapshot
Peers host chaincode and ledgers. Orderers sequence transactions. CAs and MSPs manage identity. Channels partition data.
Transaction flow (summary)
Proposal → Endorsement → Ordering → Validation → Commit → World State update.
Channel example
A private channel between two banks isolates their trades from the rest of the consortium.
Explore Key Topics
Peers: Roles
Ordering & Raft
Channels & Privacy

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify the core Fabric components and explain their responsibilities in a permissioned network. First, you will describe peer roles — endorsing, committing, and anchor — and explain how endorsement policies determine which peers must sign a proposal. Second, you will explain how an ordering service sequences transactions and why Raft is used for crash fault tolerance. Third, you will articulate how identity is managed with Certificate Authorities and how Membership Service Providers map identities to roles and permissions. Finally, you will explain channels as isolated ledgers that provide data privacy between specific organizations. Each objective couples knowledge with an applied skill: for example, tracing a transaction across peers and the orderer, or designing a simple channel topology for a two-party trade. These skills matter because good architectural choices affect privacy, scalability, and governance in production Fabric networks. We'll present small visual mnemonics and a verified competency milestone for each objective so you can check your understanding practically as you work through the lessons.

screens.title: Peers: The Workhorses of Fabric
screens.narratorSegment: Peers are the primary network nodes that host ledger copies and instances of chaincode and therefore are central to the execution and storage aspects of Fabric. Define a peer as an entity that can execute chaincode, simulate transactions, maintain a copy of the blockchain, and store the current world state. Peers do not by themselves decide transaction order; that is the job of the ordering service. In practice, organizations deploy multiple peers for resilience and role separation. For example, a manufacturing company might run an endorsing peer to validate supply-chain rules and a set of committing peers to keep resilient ledger copies. A common misconception is to assume every peer must endorse every transaction. That is false — only peers specified by an endorsement policy must simulate and sign a proposal. Another common confusion is believing peers perform consensus ordering; peers validate and commit but do not establish the canonical order. Remember the separation: peers execute and store; orderers sequence. A practical check: if you need to scale read-heavy queries, you add more committing peers or tune the world state database; if you need faster endorsement, add endorsing capacity or adjust endorsement policies. Can you now identify why splitting roles across peers helps governance and scaling?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Peers: The Workhorses
Core Concept

Peers host chaincode and ledgers

A peer executes chaincode simulations, holds a blockchain copy for history, and stores the world state for efficient queries. They are the primary runtime for business logic.

Definition
A peer is a network node that hosts ledgers and chaincode and participates in validation and commit of transactions.
Concrete example
Org1 runs a peer that endorses purchase-order chaincode and keeps copies of the blockchain to audit past orders.
Common misconception
Peers do not determine transaction order. Ordering is a separate service that sequences transactions before peers commit them.
Key Takeaway

Peers execute chaincode simulations and hold ledger data; separate roles allow scaling and clear governance.

Peer roles overview
Endorsing peer (summary)
Simulates chaincode for a proposal and signs the result if it meets policy — this provides cryptographic proof of simulation.
Committing peer (summary)
Validates ordered transactions, checks endorsements and read/write sets, then appends blocks to the ledger and updates the world state.
Anchor peer (summary)
Acts as the organization's discovery point for gossip and facilitates cross-organization peer discovery.
Real-world note
Separate endorsing and committing roles when you want to limit which peers hold signing keys or to scale query performance with additional committing peers.

screens.title: Endorsing Peers and Endorsement Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Endorsing peers play a critical role in Fabric’s transaction model: they receive proposals from client applications, simulate chaincode execution without updating the ledger, and produce signed endorsements when the simulation result meets policy. Concretely, a client sends a proposal to the set of endorsing peers specified by the chaincode’s endorsement policy. Each endorsing peer runs the chaincode logic against its current world state to produce a read/write set and a simulated response. If the simulation succeeds, the peer cryptographically signs the proposal response and returns it to the client. The client then assembles endorsements and sends a transaction to the ordering service. An important practical point is that not all peers are endorsers; endorsement is an explicit decision configured for a chaincode and organization. A common misconception is that endorsements immediately change the ledger — they do not. Endorsements are proof that a simulation result was produced under a valid state snapshot. A concrete example: if a transfer chaincode requires endorsements from both buyer and seller organizations, then both their endorsing peers must simulate and sign the proposal before the transaction can be ordered. Think about endorsement policies as governance rules encoded outside the chaincode that control which organizations must agree before a state change is allowed.

keyIdea.title: Endorsement is simulation + signature
keyIdea.text: Endorsing peers simulate chaincode and sign the result; endorsements prove a valid simulation, not a committed change.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Endorsing Peers
Endorsement process
1. Client proposal
A client sends a transaction proposal to configured endorsing peers for the chaincode.
2. Simulation
Each endorsing peer runs the chaincode against its world state snapshot to produce a read/write set and response.
3. Signing
If simulation succeeds, the peer signs the proposal response and returns it to the client as an endorsement.
4. Assembly
The client assembles endorsements and submits the transaction to the ordering service.
Concrete example
A purchase requires endorsements from both buyer and seller endorsing peers; both must simulate the transfer and sign before the orderer sequences the transaction.
Supporting notes
  • Endorsement policies are defined per chaincode and control which organizations’ peers must endorse.
  • Endorsing peers use a snapshot of the world state to ensure simulation determinism.
  • Endorsements are cryptographic proof of simulation results, not ledger commits.
Key Takeaway

Configure endorsement policies to reflect governance: only required organizations should be asked to endorse every transaction.

screens.title: Committing Peers and the World State
screens.narratorSegment: Committing peers are every peer that participates in a channel: they receive ordered blocks, validate the transactions inside, append the blocks to the blockchain, and update the world state accordingly. Define a committing peer as the node that ensures the integrity of ordered data by re-checking endorsement signatures, verifying that read/write sets still make sense, and then persisting the block. The validation step is important because the world state could have changed between endorsement and ordering; committing peers detect conflicts using the read/write sets and reject or mark transactions as invalid when necessary. A concrete example: if an endorsing peer simulated that an account had balance 100 and produced a write that subtracts 30, but another committed transaction already reduced the balance to 50 before ordering, the committing peer will detect the mismatch in the read set and mark the later transaction invalid. A common mistake is expecting world state to be authoritative history; it is a mutable snapshot optimized for queries. The blockchain stores full history. Operationally, scale committing peers to increase read availability and use a robust world state database to support rich queries. What does this separation suggest about auditing and query strategies?

keyIdea.title: Validation and persistence
keyIdea.text: Committing peers validate ordered transactions against endorsements and read/write sets, then persist blocks and update world state.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Committing Peers
Role and responsibilities
Committing peers take ordered blocks and run validation before appending to the blockchain and updating the world state. They enforce endorsement checks and detect read/write conflicts.
Validation steps
  1. Verify endorsements against policy.
  2. Check read/write sets for state conflicts.
  3. Mark transactions valid or invalid.
  4. Append the block to the blockchain and update world state for valid transactions.
Concrete scenario
Two transfer transactions touched the same account. The first committed; the second is invalidated at commit time because the read set no longer matches the current state.
Key Takeaway

World state is a mutable snapshot for queries; the blockchain is the immutable history. Committing peers ensure consistency between them.

Visual: commit check
Read/Write set conflict
Committing peers compare the read set captured during endorsement with the current world state before applying the write set.
Operational note
Add committing peers to increase read availability and use an appropriate world state database for the query patterns your application needs.
Pitfall
Assuming endorsement implies commit. Endorsements are necessary but not sufficient; committing peers perform final validation.

screens.title: Anchor Peers and Cross-Organization Discovery
screens.narratorSegment: Anchor peers are a special designation for a committing peer within an organization that enables other organizations to discover and communicate with that organization’s peers. They are not functionally different in execution or storage; instead, they serve as discovery points used by the gossip protocol to route messages and propagate ledger updates across organizational boundaries. Practical use: when Org1 and Org2 share a channel, Org1 advertises one or more anchor peers so remote organizations can find Org1’s peers and establish gossip connections. This matters for network connectivity, efficient block dissemination, and private data sharing in Fabric’s private data feature. A common mistake is to think an anchor peer holds private keys or special privileges — it does not; it simply participates in gossip and is advertised in the channel configuration to facilitate peer discovery. Misconfiguring or failing to configure anchor peers can lead to poor propagation of state and discovery failures between peers of different organizations, so ensure the channel configuration advertises reachable and resilient anchor peers. Consider redundancy and network placement: choose anchor peers that are stable and reachable across the consortium.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Anchor Peers
Purpose
Anchor peers are advertised endpoints that enable other organizations to discover and connect to an organization's peers via gossip. They are configuration entries in a channel's settings.
Concrete example
Org2 advertises two anchor peers so Org1 can discover them and exchange blocks and private data on their shared channel.
Misconception
Anchor peers are not special in cryptographic capability; they are ordinary peers chosen for reachability and discovery roles.
Operational guidance
  • Advertise reachable, stable peers as anchors in channel configuration.
  • Provide redundancy: multiple anchors reduce single-point failures for discovery.
  • Ensure network rules allow gossip traffic between anchors across organizations.
Why it matters
Proper anchor configuration ensures peers learn about each other and receive timely block propagation, which is essential for consistent state across the channel.

screens.title: Ordering Service and Raft Consensus
screens.narratorSegment: The ordering service collects transactions that clients submit after endorsement and produces a globally consistent sequence of blocks that committing peers consume. Think of the orderer as the sequencer: it does not execute chaincode and does not hold world state; its only job is to decide a canonical order for transactions. Fabric supports several ordering implementations, with Raft commonly used in production. Raft implements a leader-follower model where a leader is elected to accept and order transactions; followers replicate the leader’s decisions. If the leader becomes unavailable, Raft elects a new leader so ordering remains available under crash faults. A practical example: in a three-node Raft cluster, each ordering node replicates blocks; if one node crashes, the two remaining nodes can still form a majority and continue ordering. A common misunderstanding is to conflate consensus for ordering with endorsement-based validation. Endorsement proves simulation correctness; Raft provides crash fault-tolerant agreement on order. Operationally you should distribute Raft nodes across reliable infrastructure and tune leader placement for latency. Also avoid overloads on the orderer by keeping heavy computation off the ordering layer. How would you place Raft nodes for high availability in a multi-organization consortium?

keyIdea.text: Orderers provide a single, immutable transaction order. Raft uses leader election and replication to tolerate crashes and preserve availability.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Ordering Service & Raft
Ordering service responsibilities
Collect endorsed transactions, decide a canonical chronological order, group them into blocks, and broadcast blocks to channel peers. It has no execution role.
Raft at a glance
Leader-follower replication. Leader orders transactions; followers replicate. Leader failure triggers election.
Concrete example
Three ordering nodes replicate ordered blocks; if the leader fails, the remaining nodes elect a new leader and continue ordering.
Operational guidance
  • Place Raft nodes across reliable hosts and availability zones to tolerate crashes.
  • Keep heavy processing off the ordering service to avoid bottlenecks.
  • Monitor leader health and replication lag so you can respond to elections quickly.
Misconception
Raft orders transactions but does not validate application logic — validation still occurs at committing peers using endorsement evidence.
Key Takeaway

Use Raft to provide crash tolerance for ordering. Keep ordering focused on sequencing rather than execution.

screens.title: Certificate Authorities and MSPs
screens.narratorSegment: Identity management in Fabric has two complementary parts: Certificate Authorities issue cryptographic certificates that prove identity, and Membership Service Providers define how those certificates map to roles and permissions inside an organization. A Certificate Authority is responsible for onboarding participants by issuing X.509 certificates that peers and users present when interacting with the network. The MSP is a policy layer: it specifies which certificate authorities are trusted for an organization and how to interpret attributes on certificates to grant roles. For example, Org1’s CA issues a certificate to a new peer or user; Org1’s MSP configuration says that certificates signed by that CA correspond to Org1 identities and maps certain certificate attributes to roles like admin or peer. A common misconception is to treat the CA as an authorization mechanism by itself — CAs only attest identity; authorization is enforced by MSP rules and channel policies. Operationally, maintain CA security, rotate certificates prudently, and ensure MSP configurations accurately reflect trust anchors. A concrete scenario: when adding a new organization to a channel, its MSP is added to channel configuration so other members can validate its certificates. How would you design CA and MSP roles to separate enrollment from operational authorization?

keyIdea.text: CAs issue certificates that prove identity; MSPs define how those identities map to organizational roles and permissions.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › CAs & MSPs
Certificate Authority (CA)
Issues digital certificates that establish verifiable identities for organizations, peers, and users. These certificates are used for TLS and signing transactions.
Concrete example
Org1’s CA issues a certificate to a new peer; that certificate proves the peer’s identity to other network participants.
Membership Service Provider (MSP)
Defines the set of trusted CAs and rules that map identities to roles and permissions within an organization and channel context.
Operational note
When adding an organization to a channel, include its MSP so other members can validate its certificates and trust anchors.
Misconception
A CA does not grant permissions by itself. Authorization is enforced by MSP configuration and channel policies that interpret certificate attributes.
Key Takeaway

Keep certificate issuance and MSP trust anchors well managed: they form the basis of permissioned governance in Fabric.

screens.title: Channels: Private, Isolated Ledgers
screens.narratorSegment: Channels provide strict data partitioning in Hyperledger Fabric by creating private ledgers that connect a subset of participants. Each channel maintains its own blockchain and world state, so transactions on one channel are not visible to organizations that are not part of that channel. This allows consortia to operate multiple collaboration contexts in the same underlying network while preserving confidentiality for sensitive transactions. A practical example: in a financial consortium, a subset of banks may form a private channel to exchange trade data that must remain confidential, while governance and general member interactions can occur on a different, consortium-wide channel. Channels are configured with their own channel configuration, policies, and MSP sets; adding or removing organizations requires channel configuration updates. A common misconception is to treat channels as simple access lists; they are full ledgers with independent state. When designing channels, balance the overhead of managing multiple ledgers against the privacy benefits — too many channels increase operational complexity, while too few reduce confidentiality. Consider whether private data collections or channels better meet the confidentiality and complexity trade-offs for your use case.

keyIdea.text: Channels create independent ledgers for a subset of participants, enforcing transaction privacy between those organizations.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Channels
What a channel is
A channel is a private blockchain between a subset of network participants. Each channel has its own ledger, chaincode definitions, and policies, isolating data from others.
Concrete example
Org1 and Org2 form a channel for bilateral trade data; Org3 is not a member and cannot see transactions on that channel.
Operational note
Channels reduce disclosure but increase management overhead. Evaluate whether private data collections or channels better meet your privacy and complexity trade-offs.
Channel configuration and governance
Each channel has policies that control membership changes and endorsement rules. MSPs for channel members are included in the channel config so members can validate identities.
Misconception
Channels are not just ACLs — they create independent ledgers with their own history and world state.
Key Takeaway

Use channels to isolate sensitive transactions between specific organizations, balancing privacy against operational complexity.

screens.title: Chaincode: Smart Contracts in Fabric
screens.narratorSegment: Chaincode is Fabric’s term for smart contracts: code that implements business rules and manipulates ledger state. When a client invokes chaincode, endorsing peers simulate the chaincode’s execution to produce a read/write set and result without committing changes. Chaincode can be written in supported languages and deployed to peers, and endorsement policies determine which organizations’ endorsing peers must run that chaincode for a transaction to be valid. Importantly, chaincode itself should not assume it runs only on one peer; simulation determinism is key. If chaincode relies on external mutable data or non-deterministic operations, endorsements may diverge and transactions will fail validation. A concrete example: an inventory chaincode decreases stock when a sale is proposed; endorsing peers simulate the stock decrement and produce a write set. At commit time, committing peers verify the read set still matches the world state. A common pitfall is embedding access-control decisions in chaincode that should instead be expressed through endorsement and channel policies; keep chaincode focused on business logic and use MSP/policy configuration for governance. How will you design chaincode to be deterministic and policy-aware? Chaincode: Smart Contracts in Fabric means chaincode simulates state transitions; keep it deterministic and let policies enforce who must endorse and who may access the results.. In practical terms, chaincode encapsulates business logic and how it is used during endorsement and commit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Chaincode simulates state transitions; keep it deterministic and let policies enforce who must endorse and who may access the results.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Chaincode
What chaincode does
Encapsulates the business logic that generates state changes represented as read/write sets. Endorsing peers simulate chaincode; committing peers apply validated write sets to the world state.
Concrete example
An inventory chaincode reduces stock on a sale. Endorsers simulate and return the write set; commit applies it if validation succeeds.
Determinism requirement
Avoid non-deterministic operations or external mutable references during simulation, since differing simulations cause endorsement mismatches.
Design guidance
  • Keep chaincode focused on business logic and state transitions.
  • Use endorsement policies and MSPs to express governance and access controls.
  • Test chaincode determinism across endorsers to avoid validation failures.
Key Takeaway

Chaincode provides deterministic business logic; pair it with well-defined endorsement policies to enforce governance.

screens.title: Ledger: Blockchain vs World State
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric’s ledger has two complementary components: the blockchain, an immutable append-only history of ordered and validated transactions, and the world state, a mutable database that stores current asset values for efficient queries. The blockchain provides full auditability and traceability — every transaction ever ordered and validated is preserved in sequence. The world state, by contrast, is a snapshot optimized for read performance; it holds the latest values and can be implemented with LevelDB or CouchDB depending on query needs. A concrete example: when a user's balance changes, the blockchain records the transaction that caused it, while the world state reflects the new balance for quick lookups. A common mistake is to rely on the world state for historical audits — you must consult the blockchain to reconstruct history. Operationally, choose the world state database that supports your query patterns: CouchDB supports rich JSON queries; LevelDB is a fast key-value option. Also remember that updates to the world state only occur after a transaction is validated and committed by committing peers. How will you use the blockchain for auditing and the world state for real-time queries in your application?

keyIdea.text: The blockchain is the immutable history used for audits; the world state is a mutable snapshot used for efficient current-value queries.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Ledger: Blockchain vs World State
Blockchain (immutable history)
Append-only set of blocks containing ordered and validated transactions. Used for auditing, replay, and provenance.
Use case
Audit trails and forensic inspection of how asset values evolved over time.
World State (mutable snapshot)
Current view of asset values stored as a key-value database for efficient queries. Updated only upon commit of validated transactions.
Database options
LevelDB for simple key-value needs; CouchDB for rich JSON queries and ad-hoc lookups.
Key Takeaway

Use the blockchain for complete history and the world state for fast current-value queries; do not substitute one for the other.

screens.title: Transaction Flow and Hands-on Analysis
screens.narratorSegment: Let's trace a typical transaction end-to-end to solidify how Fabric components cooperate. Start with a client application that constructs a proposal to invoke chaincode and sends it to the endorsing peers specified by the endorsement policy. Each endorsing peer simulates execution and returns a signed endorsement containing a read/write set. The client collects the required endorsements and submits the assembled transaction to the ordering service. The orderer sequences transactions into blocks and broadcasts them to all committing peers on the channel. Committing peers validate each transaction by checking endorsements and read/write sets against the current world state; valid transactions are appended to the blockchain and applied to update the world state, while invalid ones are recorded as invalid but still preserved in the block for audit. A concrete scenario: Org1’s client proposes a transfer requiring both Org1 and Org2 endorsements; both endorsers sign; the orderer sequences the transaction; committing peers verify and the transfer is reflected in all channel members’ world states. A common misconception to avoid: orders are not endorsements and endorsements are not commits. Practice labeling a three-organization diagram and narrating this flow back as a verification exercise.

keyIdea.title: End-to-end flow
keyIdea.text: Proposal → Endorsement → Ordering → Validation → Commit; each component contributes a specific responsibility to maintain correctness and privacy.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Transaction Flow
Step-by-step
1. Proposal
Client sends a proposal to endorsing peers to simulate chaincode.
2. Endorsement
Endorsing peers simulate and sign proposal responses with read/write sets.
3. Ordering
Client submits assembled endorsements to orderer, which sequences transactions into blocks.
4. Validation & Commit
Committing peers validate endorsements and read/write sets, append blocks, and update world state for valid transactions.
Hands-on activity
Label a network diagram: place an endorsing peer for Org1, a committing peer for Org2, the ordering service, and the channel between Org1 and Org2. Then narrate the transaction path from client to commit.
Compact flow
Proposal → Endorse → Assemble → Order → Validate → Commit → Update world state.
Pitfall to avoid
Do not expect endorsements to guarantee commit; validation at commit time may reject transactions if state changed since endorsement.
Key Takeaway

Tracing the full flow helps reveal where privacy, validation, and ordering responsibilities live and how to design resilient topologies.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These three key concepts summarize the core architectural ideas you should retain. First, peers are the execution and storage layer: they simulate chaincode, endorse proposals when configured, and commit validated transactions to the ledger. Second, the ordering service sequences transactions but does not execute chaincode or hold world state; Raft provides crash fault tolerance through leader election and replication. Third, identity is managed by certificate authorities while MSPs express how identities map to roles and permissions; treat CAs as identity issuers and MSPs as the policy layer that enforces trust. Each of these points affects a design decision: where to place workload, how to configure trust, and how to partition data for privacy. Keep these short statements handy when you design a Fabric network or explain its architecture to stakeholders.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we map the essential components that make Hyperledger Fabric a modular, permissioned blockchain platform. You will learn what peers do, how endorsing and committing roles differ, why anchor peers matter for cross-organization communication, and how the ordering service establishes a single, immutable sequence of transactions without executing business logic. We'll also explain identity management via Certificate Authorities and Membership Service Providers, the purpose of channels for private data partitioning, and how chaincode and the ledger interact to represent business logic and state. A concrete example you'll use throughout is a two-organization channel where both organizations must endorse a trade: we will trace a transaction from proposal to endorsement, through ordering and finally to ledger commit and world state update. Common misunderstandings we’ll clear up include confusing ordering with execution, and assuming channels are mere access controls rather than separate ledgers. By the end you should be able to describe each component’s responsibility and reason about a basic Fabric topology for a consortium. Consider how these pieces separate concerns: identity, execution, ordering, and storage — why is that helpful for governance and scaling?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify the core Fabric components and explain their responsibilities in a permissioned network. First, you will describe peer roles — endorsing, committing, and anchor — and explain how endorsement policies determine which peers must sign a proposal. Second, you will explain how an ordering service sequences transactions and why Raft is used for crash fault tolerance. Third, you will articulate how identity is managed with Certificate Authorities and how Membership Service Providers map identities to roles and permissions. Finally, you will explain channels as isolated ledgers that provide data privacy between specific organizations. Each objective couples knowledge with an applied skill: for example, tracing a transaction across peers and the orderer, or designing a simple channel topology for a two-party trade. These skills matter because good architectural choices affect privacy, scalability, and governance in production Fabric networks. We'll present small visual mnemonics and a verified competency milestone for each objective so you can check your understanding practically as you work through the lessons.

These second objectives focus on applied abilities you will practice in the lab walkthrough. First, you will trace a full transaction from a client proposal, through endorsement, ordering, validation, and commit, and explain what each component contributes. Second, you will design a minimal channel topology to protect sensitive data between two organizations while keeping governance for a consortium. Third, you will inspect ledger components and explain the difference between the immutable blockchain and the mutable world state, and when each is used during queries. Fourth, you will recognize common architectural pitfalls — for example, overloading the orderer with non-essential tasks, confusing endorsement with ordering, or misconfiguring anchor peers so gossip cannot bridge organizations. Each card includes a brief mnemonic and a verified milestone so you can test your understanding by labeling a sample network diagram and narrating a transaction flow back to a peer. These applied skills are what shift knowledge into operational capability for deploying and operating Fabric networks.

Peers are the primary network nodes that host ledger copies and instances of chaincode and therefore are central to the execution and storage aspects of Fabric. Define a peer as an entity that can execute chaincode, simulate transactions, maintain a copy of the blockchain, and store the current world state. Peers do not by themselves decide transaction order; that is the job of the ordering service. In practice, organizations deploy multiple peers for resilience and role separation. For example, a manufacturing company might run an endorsing peer to validate supply-chain rules and a set of committing peers to keep resilient ledger copies. A common misconception is to assume every peer must endorse every transaction. That is false — only peers specified by an endorsement policy must simulate and sign a proposal. Another common confusion is believing peers perform consensus ordering; peers validate and commit but do not establish the canonical order. Remember the separation: peers execute and store; orderers sequence. A practical check: if you need to scale read-heavy queries, you add more committing peers or tune the world state database; if you need faster endorsement, add endorsing capacity or adjust endorsement policies. Can you now identify why splitting roles across peers helps governance and scaling?

Endorsing peers play a critical role in Fabric’s transaction model: they receive proposals from client applications, simulate chaincode execution without updating the ledger, and produce signed endorsements when the simulation result meets policy. Concretely, a client sends a proposal to the set of endorsing peers specified by the chaincode’s endorsement policy. Each endorsing peer runs the chaincode logic against its current world state to produce a read/write set and a simulated response. If the simulation succeeds, the peer cryptographically signs the proposal response and returns it to the client. The client then assembles endorsements and sends a transaction to the ordering service. An important practical point is that not all peers are endorsers; endorsement is an explicit decision configured for a chaincode and organization. A common misconception is that endorsements immediately change the ledger — they do not. Endorsements are proof that a simulation result was produced under a valid state snapshot. A concrete example: if a transfer chaincode requires endorsements from both buyer and seller organizations, then both their endorsing peers must simulate and sign the proposal before the transaction can be ordered. Think about endorsement policies as governance rules encoded outside the chaincode that control which organizations must agree before a state change is allowed.

Committing peers are every peer that participates in a channel: they receive ordered blocks, validate the transactions inside, append the blocks to the blockchain, and update the world state accordingly. Define a committing peer as the node that ensures the integrity of ordered data by re-checking endorsement signatures, verifying that read/write sets still make sense, and then persisting the block. The validation step is important because the world state could have changed between endorsement and ordering; committing peers detect conflicts using the read/write sets and reject or mark transactions as invalid when necessary. A concrete example: if an endorsing peer simulated that an account had balance 100 and produced a write that subtracts 30, but another committed transaction already reduced the balance to 50 before ordering, the committing peer will detect the mismatch in the read set and mark the later transaction invalid. A common mistake is expecting world state to be authoritative history; it is a mutable snapshot optimized for queries. The blockchain stores full history. Operationally, scale committing peers to increase read availability and use a robust world state database to support rich queries. What does this separation suggest about auditing and query strategies?

Anchor peers are a special designation for a committing peer within an organization that enables other organizations to discover and communicate with that organization’s peers. They are not functionally different in execution or storage; instead, they serve as discovery points used by the gossip protocol to route messages and propagate ledger updates across organizational boundaries. Practical use: when Org1 and Org2 share a channel, Org1 advertises one or more anchor peers so remote organizations can find Org1’s peers and establish gossip connections. This matters for network connectivity, efficient block dissemination, and private data sharing in Fabric’s private data feature. A common mistake is to think an anchor peer holds private keys or special privileges — it does not; it simply participates in gossip and is advertised in the channel configuration to facilitate peer discovery. Misconfiguring or failing to configure anchor peers can lead to poor propagation of state and discovery failures between peers of different organizations, so ensure the channel configuration advertises reachable and resilient anchor peers. Consider redundancy and network placement: choose anchor peers that are stable and reachable across the consortium.

The ordering service collects transactions that clients submit after endorsement and produces a globally consistent sequence of blocks that committing peers consume. Think of the orderer as the sequencer: it does not execute chaincode and does not hold world state; its only job is to decide a canonical order for transactions. Fabric supports several ordering implementations, with Raft commonly used in production. Raft implements a leader-follower model where a leader is elected to accept and order transactions; followers replicate the leader’s decisions. If the leader becomes unavailable, Raft elects a new leader so ordering remains available under crash faults. A practical example: in a three-node Raft cluster, each ordering node replicates blocks; if one node crashes, the two remaining nodes can still form a majority and continue ordering. A common misunderstanding is to conflate consensus for ordering with endorsement-based validation. Endorsement proves simulation correctness; Raft provides crash fault-tolerant agreement on order. Operationally you should distribute Raft nodes across reliable infrastructure and tune leader placement for latency. Also avoid overloads on the orderer by keeping heavy computation off the ordering layer. How would you place Raft nodes for high availability in a multi-organization consortium?

Identity management in Fabric has two complementary parts: Certificate Authorities issue cryptographic certificates that prove identity, and Membership Service Providers define how those certificates map to roles and permissions inside an organization. A Certificate Authority is responsible for onboarding participants by issuing X.509 certificates that peers and users present when interacting with the network. The MSP is a policy layer: it specifies which certificate authorities are trusted for an organization and how to interpret attributes on certificates to grant roles. For example, Org1’s CA issues a certificate to a new peer or user; Org1’s MSP configuration says that certificates signed by that CA correspond to Org1 identities and maps certain certificate attributes to roles like admin or peer. A common misconception is to treat the CA as an authorization mechanism by itself — CAs only attest identity; authorization is enforced by MSP rules and channel policies. Operationally, maintain CA security, rotate certificates prudently, and ensure MSP configurations accurately reflect trust anchors. A concrete scenario: when adding a new organization to a channel, its MSP is added to channel configuration so other members can validate its certificates. How would you design CA and MSP roles to separate enrollment from operational authorization?

Channels provide strict data partitioning in Hyperledger Fabric by creating private ledgers that connect a subset of participants. Each channel maintains its own blockchain and world state, so transactions on one channel are not visible to organizations that are not part of that channel. This allows consortia to operate multiple collaboration contexts in the same underlying network while preserving confidentiality for sensitive transactions. A practical example: in a financial consortium, a subset of banks may form a private channel to exchange trade data that must remain confidential, while governance and general member interactions can occur on a different, consortium-wide channel. Channels are configured with their own channel configuration, policies, and MSP sets; adding or removing organizations requires channel configuration updates. A common misconception is to treat channels as simple access lists; they are full ledgers with independent state. When designing channels, balance the overhead of managing multiple ledgers against the privacy benefits — too many channels increase operational complexity, while too few reduce confidentiality.
